blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a concerning vulnerability in reading comprehension systems exposed by Jia & Liang's paper. While state-of-the-art models achieve high accuracy (84.7% F1) on the SQuAD dataset, their performance collapses to just 36% when adversarially perturbed with a single grammatically correct but semantically distracting sentence. Even more alarmingly, model-independent adversarial additions (AddOneSent) reduce accuracy from 80% to 2.7%, revealing that these systems rely heavily on shallow pattern matching rather than true understanding. The paper demonstrates that models are overly stable, failing to recognize how small perturbations can alter meaning, unlike image-based adversarial attacks which exploit oversensitivity. The authors propose systematic methods (AddSent, AddAny) to generate adversarial examples while preserving grammatical correctness and answer validity, showing these attacks generalize across 16 different models. Human performance remains robust against these perturbations, underscoring the models' superficial reliance on surface-level features.
paper_title: Adversarial examples for evaluating reading comprehension systems
paper_abstract: Standard accuracy metrics indicate that reading comprehension systems are making rapid progress, but the extent to which these systems truly understand language remains unclear. To reward systems with real language understanding abilities, we propose an adversarial evaluation scheme for the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD). Our method tests whether systems can answer questions about paragraphs that contain adversarially inserted sentences, which are automatically generated to distract computer systems without changing the correct answer or misleading humans. In this adversarial setting, the accuracy of sixteen published models drops from an average of 75% F1 score to 36%; when the adversary is allowed to add ungrammatical sequences of words, average accuracy on four models decreases further to 7%. We hope our insights will motivate the development of new models that understand language more precisely.
